title: Sherlock Holmes: The Red-Headed League
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
ru: Холмс расследует странную работу для рыжих мужчин и раскрывает план ограбления банка

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Man with Fiery Red Hair
chapters.text:
One Saturday in autumn I called on my friend Sherlock Holmes in Baker Street. I found him deep in conversation with a fat, elderly gentleman whose hair was the brightest red I had ever seen. I apologized and turned to go, but Holmes jumped up, pulled me into the room and shut the door.

“You could not have come at a better time, my dear Watson,” he said. “Mr Wilson, this is Dr Watson. He has helped me in many of my cases, and he may be useful in yours. Please tell your story again from the beginning. My friend has not heard it, and I want to hear every detail twice.”

While our visitor searched in his coat, I tried to read him in my friend's way. I learned very little. He was an ordinary London businessman, slow and rather pleased with himself, in old, not very clean clothes. A heavy chain hung across his waistcoat, with a little coin on it that had a square hole in the middle. Apart from his blazing red hair, there was nothing special about him.

Holmes saw what I was doing and smiled.

“I can tell you only the obvious facts,” he said. “Mr Wilson has done hard work with his hands at some time. He has been to China. And he has done a lot of writing lately. Apart from that, I know nothing.”

Mr Wilson sat up straight. “How in the world did you know all that, Mr Holmes? It's true I started life as a ship's carpenter. But how?”

“Your right hand is a whole size larger than your left. You have worked with it, so the muscles are bigger.”

“And China?”

“There is a fish tattooed just above your wrist. Only in China do they colour the scales of a fish that delicate pink. And there is a Chinese coin on your watch chain, which makes it even simpler.”

“And the writing?”

“The cuff of your right sleeve is very shiny, and there is a smooth patch on your left elbow, where it rests on the desk.”

Mr Wilson laughed loudly. “Well, I never! I thought at first you had done something clever. But I see there was nothing in it after all.”

“I begin to think, Watson,” said Holmes, “that I make a mistake when I explain. Now, Mr Wilson, have you found the advertisement?”

“Here it is.” He put a thick red finger on a page of an old newspaper. “This is where it all began. Read it, doctor.”

I read aloud:

“TO THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE. There is now another vacancy for a member of the League. The pay is four pounds a week for very easy work. All red-headed men who are over twenty-one and healthy in body and mind may apply. Come in person on Monday at eleven o'clock to Duncan Ross, at the offices of the League, 7 Pope's Court, Fleet Street.”

“What on earth does this mean?” I asked.

Holmes laughed quietly. “It is a little unusual, isn't it? Go on, Mr Wilson. Tell us about yourself and your business.”

“I have a small pawnbroker's shop in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City,” said Mr Wilson. “People leave their watches and rings with me, and I lend them money. Business has been bad for years. I have only one assistant, and I couldn't even afford him, but he agreed to work for half the usual wages so that he could learn the trade.”

“Half wages?” said Holmes. “That is unusual. What is his name?”

“Vincent Spaulding. He's very clever, Mr Holmes. He could earn twice as much somewhere else. But if he's happy, why should I put ideas into his head? He has only one fault. He's crazy about photography. He's always running down into the cellar, like a rabbit into its hole, to develop his pictures.”

Holmes said nothing, but his eyes closed a little, as if he was putting the cellar away somewhere safe in his mind.

“We lived very quietly,” Mr Wilson went on, “until one morning eight weeks ago. Spaulding came into the shop with this very paper in his hand, and he said, ‘Oh, Mr Wilson, I wish I was a red-headed man!’”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. A Job for Red-Headed Men
chapters.text:
“‘Why?’ I asked him,” said Mr Wilson. “‘Because there's a vacancy in the Red-Headed League,’ he said. ‘It's a small fortune for any man who gets it.’

“I had never heard of the League. I'm a man who stays at home, Mr Holmes. Sometimes I don't go out for weeks. Spaulding explained it all. An American millionaire called Ezekiah Hopkins had red hair himself, and when he died, he left all his money to help men with hair like his. The pay was good and the work was almost nothing.

“‘But there must be millions of red-headed men,’ I said.

“‘Not as many as you think,’ he answered. ‘You must live in London and be a grown man. And your hair must be bright, fiery red, like yours. You only have to walk in, Mr Wilson. The job is yours.’

“Well, gentlemen, an extra two hundred pounds a year would be very useful. So we closed the shop and went to Fleet Street.

“I hope I never see a sight like it again. Every man in London with a little red in his hair had come. Fleet Street was full of them, and Pope's Court looked like a cart of oranges. There was every colour you can imagine: straw, lemon, orange, brick, clay. I wanted to give up and go home, but Spaulding pushed and pulled me through the crowd, right up the steps and into the office.

“There was nothing there but two wooden chairs and a table. Behind the table sat a small man whose hair was even redder than mine. He said a few words to each man and always found something wrong with him. But when our turn came, he shut the door and looked at me for a long time.

“‘This is Mr Jabez Wilson,’ said Spaulding, ‘and he would like to join the League.’

“‘And he is perfect for it,’ said the little man. ‘I have never seen anything so fine.’ Suddenly he took my hair in both hands and pulled until I shouted with pain. ‘There are tears in your eyes,’ he said, as he let go. ‘Forgive me, but we must be careful. Twice we have been tricked by wigs, and once by paint.’ Then he went to the window and called down that the vacancy was filled. A long, sad groan came up from the street, and all the red heads went off in different directions.

“‘My name is Duncan Ross,’ he said. ‘The hours are ten to two. You must stay in this office the whole time. If you leave the building even once, you lose the job forever. Your work is to copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica.’ That's the huge set of books that explains everything in the world, from A to Z.

“I said I had a shop to look after. ‘Don't worry about that,’ said Spaulding. ‘I'll look after it for you.’ And it's true that a pawnbroker is busiest in the evenings, especially just before payday, so the morning hours suited me well.

“I went home very happy. By the evening, however, I felt low again. It all seemed too strange to be true. But the next morning I bought ink, a pen and paper and went to Pope's Court. Mr Ross was there. He started me on the letter A and came in now and then to check on me.

“That went on day after day for eight weeks, Mr Holmes. Every Saturday Mr Ross put four gold sovereigns — four pounds — on my table. After a while he stopped coming in at all, except on Saturdays, but I never dared to leave the room. I wrote about Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture, and I hoped to reach the B's soon. And then the whole thing came to an end.”

“To an end?”

“Yes, sir. This very morning. I went to work as usual, but the door was locked, and a little square of card was nailed to it. Here it is.”

He held it up. It said:

THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890.

Holmes and I looked at the card and at the sad, serious face behind it. The whole thing was so ridiculous that we both burst out laughing.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Knees of His Trousers
chapters.text:
“I can't see anything funny about it!” cried Mr Wilson, and his face went as red as his hair. He stood up to leave.

“No, no,” said Holmes, and he pushed him gently back into the chair. “I wouldn't miss your case for the world. But it is a little funny, you must admit. What did you do when you found the card?”

“I asked the landlord downstairs. He had never heard of the League or of Duncan Ross. But when I described the man, he said it must be a lawyer called William Morris, who had moved out yesterday. He gave me the new address, 17 King Edward Street. I went there at once. It was a factory that makes artificial knees, and nobody had heard of William Morris or Duncan Ross.”

“And then?”

“Then I came to you. I don't want to lose a job like that without a fight, Mr Holmes.”

“You have lost nothing,” said Holmes. “You are more than thirty pounds richer, and you know a lot about subjects that begin with A. But I agree that this is serious. Now, a few questions. Your assistant, who first showed you the advertisement. How long had he been with you then?”

“About a month.”

“How did he come to you?”

“He answered an advertisement I put in the paper.”

“Was he the only man who came?”

“No, there were a dozen. But he was clever, and he was cheap.”

“At half wages. Yes. What does he look like, this Vincent Spaulding?”

“Small, strong, very quick in his movements. No hair on his face, though he's not far from thirty. And he has a white mark on his forehead, where acid splashed him once.”

Holmes sat up in his chair, very excited. “I thought so,” he said. “Have you noticed that his ears are pierced for earrings?”

“Yes, sir. He told me it was done when he was a boy.”

“Hm!” said Holmes, and he sank back into deep thought. “He is still with you?”

“Oh yes. I left him at the shop just now.”

“That will do, Mr Wilson. Today is Saturday. I hope we can give you an answer by Monday.”

When our visitor had gone, Holmes turned to me. “Well, Watson, what do you make of it?”

“Nothing,” I said honestly. “It is a complete mystery.”

“As a rule, the stranger a thing is, the less mysterious it proves to be. It is the ordinary crimes that are hard to solve. But I must act quickly.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Smoke,” he answered. “It is quite a three-pipe problem. Please don't speak to me for fifty minutes.”

He curled up in his chair with his thin knees near his nose and his black pipe sticking out like the beak of a strange bird. I thought he had fallen asleep. Then suddenly he jumped up.

“Come, Watson! We are going to Saxe-Coburg Square.”

It was a poor, shabby little square, with four rows of dirty brick houses around a small garden of tired grass. Three gold balls hung over the door of a corner house, the old sign of a pawnbroker, and a board said JABEZ WILSON in white letters. Holmes walked slowly up the street and down again, looking hard at the houses. Then he stopped in front of the shop and hit the pavement two or three times, hard, with his stick. Finally he went up to the door and knocked.

It was opened at once by a bright-looking young man with a clean-shaven face.

“Excuse me,” said Holmes. “Can you tell me the way to the Strand?”

“Third on the right, fourth on the left,” said the young man quickly, and he shut the door.

“A smart fellow,” said Holmes as we walked away. “In my opinion, he is the fourth smartest man in London. I have heard of him before.”

“So Mr Wilson's assistant is an important part of this mystery,” I said. “You asked the way only so that you could see him.”

“Not him,” said Holmes. “I wanted to see the knees of his trousers.”

“And what did you see?”

“What I expected to see.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. A Game for Higher Stakes
chapters.text:
“But why did you hit the pavement?” I asked.

“My dear doctor, this is a time for watching, not for talking. We are spies in an enemy's country. We know something about Saxe-Coburg Square. Now let us look at what is behind it.”

We turned the corner, and it was like stepping into a different world. Here was one of the main roads of the City, full of carriages, cabs and busy people. A line of fine shops and offices stood along it. It was hard to believe that the quiet, shabby square was just behind them.

“Let me see,” said Holmes, looking along the row. “I like to know the exact order of the houses. Mortimer's, the tobacco shop. The little newspaper shop. The Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank. A vegetarian restaurant. McFarlane's, the carriage builders. And now, doctor, we have done our work, and it is time for play. A sandwich, a cup of coffee, and then a violin concert, where no red-headed clients will trouble us with their puzzles.”

All afternoon Holmes sat in the concert hall with a happy, dreamy smile, gently moving his long thin fingers in time to the music. Nobody looking at him could believe that this was the sharp, cold hunter of criminals. But I knew that when he looked dreamy, his mind was often working at its hardest.

“You want to go home, I suppose, doctor,” he said as we came out. “I have some business that will take a few hours. This business at Saxe-Coburg Square is serious. A big crime is being planned, and I believe we will be just in time to stop it. But today is Saturday, which makes things more difficult. I shall want your help tonight.”

“At what time?”

“Ten will be early enough.”

“I shall be at Baker Street at ten.”

“Very well. And, doctor, there may be some danger. Please put your army revolver in your pocket.” He waved his hand, turned, and disappeared into the crowd.

I walked home feeling rather stupid. I had heard and seen everything that Holmes had. But he clearly understood what had happened and what was going to happen, while to me it was all still a confused mystery. I went over the facts again. The strange job copying the encyclopaedia. An assistant who worked for half wages and spent hours in the cellar. Holmes hitting the pavement with his stick. His interest in a young man's trousers. A bank just around the corner. Where were we going tonight, and why did I need a gun? I could find no answer, so I gave up and waited for the night.

At a quarter past nine I walked across the park to Baker Street. Two cabs were standing at the door, and in Holmes's room I found two men. One was Peter Jones, a police detective from Scotland Yard. The other was a long, thin, sad-faced man with a very shiny hat.

“Our party is complete,” said Holmes, as he buttoned his coat. “Watson, this is Mr Merryweather, a director of the City and Suburban Bank. He is joining us tonight.”

“I hope this is not a wild goose chase — all this trouble for nothing,” said Mr Merryweather unhappily. “This is the first Saturday night in twenty-seven years that I have not played cards at my club.”

“You will play for higher stakes tonight than ever before,” said Holmes. “For you, sir, the stake will be thirty thousand pounds. And for you, Jones, it will be the man you want most in all England.”

“John Clay,” said Jones, “the murderer, thief and forger. He's young, Mr Merryweather, but he's at the top of his profession. His grandfather was a royal duke, and he went to the best school and to Oxford University. His brain is as quick as his fingers. We find signs of him everywhere, but we never find the man himself. I've been after him for years, and I've never even seen him.”

“I hope I can introduce you tonight,” said Holmes. “It is after ten, and time we started. Come, gentlemen. The game is ready to begin.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. A Light Under the Floor
chapters.text:
Our two cabs took us back to the busy road I had seen that afternoon. Mr Merryweather led us through a side door and down some stone steps into a huge cellar full of heavy wooden boxes.

“Nobody could get in here from below,” he said proudly, and he hit the floor with his stick. “Why — it sounds hollow!”

“Quiet, please!” said Holmes sharply. “You may ruin everything. Sit down on that box and don't move.”

Mr Merryweather sat down, looking very hurt.

“We have at least an hour,” Holmes went on. “They will not start until the good pawnbroker is safely in bed. Watson, you have guessed that we are under a bank. Mr Merryweather, tell him what is in these boxes.”

“Gold,” whispered the director. “Thirty thousand napoleons — French gold coins. We borrowed them from the Bank of France.”

“Now we must sit in the dark,” said Holmes, and he covered his lantern. “Watson, if they shoot, don't wait — shoot back. Jones has sent three men to the pawnbroker's shop. If the thieves run back through their tunnel, they will run straight into the police.”

I have never known such darkness. I could hear the heavy breathing of the bank director. It felt like the whole night, but later Holmes told me it was only an hour and a quarter.

Suddenly I saw a thin line of yellow light between the stones of the floor. Then a white hand, almost like a woman's, came up through it and felt around. With a loud crack, one of the big stones turned over, and there was a square hole. A clean-shaven young face looked out. The young man climbed out and turned to help a second man — a man with bright red hair.

“It's all clear,” he whispered. “Have you got the bags? Great Scott! Jump, Archie, jump!”

Holmes had sprung out and caught him by the collar. The red-headed man dived back down the hole, and I heard the cloth tear as Jones grabbed his coat. Suddenly there was a gun in the young man's hand, but Holmes hit his wrist with his stick, and it fell to the floor.

“It's no use, John Clay,” said Holmes quietly. “You have no chance at all.”

“So I see,” said Clay, very calmly. “But my friend has got away, I think.”

“Three men are waiting for him at the other end.”

Jones put handcuffs on him. “Don't touch me with your dirty hands,” said Clay. “I have royal blood. And please call me ‘sir’ and say ‘please’ when you speak to me.”

“All right,” laughed Jones. “Would you please, sir, walk upstairs, where we can get a cab to carry your Highness to the police station?”

“That is better,” said John Clay. He bowed to the three of us and walked quietly away with Jones.

Early in the morning, back in Baker Street, Holmes explained everything.

“It was clear from the beginning, Watson, that the League had only one purpose: to get the pawnbroker out of his shop for a few hours every day. Then I heard about the assistant who worked for half wages and spent hours in the cellar. The acid mark and the pierced ears told me he was John Clay. And the cellar told me what he was doing. He was digging a tunnel to some other building.”

“So that is why you knocked at the door?”

“Yes. I wanted to see his knees. They were worn and dirty, as they would be after weeks of digging. When I hit the pavement, the sound told me the tunnel did not run under the street in front. So it went behind the house. And when we turned the corner, there was the bank, right behind Mr Wilson's shop. When the League suddenly closed, I knew they no longer needed Mr Wilson out of the way. The tunnel was ready. Saturday night was best, because the bank is closed until Monday. That gave them two days to escape.”

“You reasoned it out beautifully,” I said.

“It saved me from boredom,” he answered with a yawn. “My life is one long effort to escape from the ordinary. These little problems help me to do so.”
